 CS Joho Restricts Diwali Fireworks to 7pm-11pm, Sets Safety Rules 
 -->
 --> 
 by Timothy Cerullo on Tuesday, 3 November 2026 - 7:15 am 
 Mining Cabinet Secretary Hassan Joho addressing the press at a past event. 
 KNA 
 -->
 Mining Cabinet Secretary Hassan Joho has announced strict regulations for fireworks displays during the upcoming three-day Diwali celebrations, which run from Friday, November 6, to Sunday, November 8, 2026. 
 In a notice dated Tuesday, November 3, Joho restricted fireworks displays to between 7pm and 11pm during the three days, warning that all activities must be orderly to avoid inconveniencing other Kenyans. 
 "The Hindu community is requested to ensure that fireworks displays are carried out within the requirements of the Explosives Act Cap 115 Laws of Kenya. Fireworks displays should be carried out in an orderly manner so that the general public are not inconvenienced," the CS announced. 
 Joho directed organisers to obtain the necessary permits from the State Department for Mining offices at Madini House in Nairobi or respective county mining offices before conducting fireworks displays. 
 A past image of fireworks lighting up Nairobi 
 Photo 
 KTN 
 He also restricted fireworks displays to authorised venues, including clubs , hotels, temples, sports grounds and school compounds, while other venues can be used only after approval from an Inspector of Explosives. 
 Joho further limited display shells to a maximum of four-inch calibre in urban and built-up areas, unless an Inspector of Explosives grants an exemption. 
 “Only qualified, experienced and sober persons shall be allowed to fire aerial shells and other aerial display fireworks,” Joho stated. 
 The Ministry also warned fireworks dealers against selling fireworks to children under 13, saying such a practice is an offence under the Explosives Act and could attract a hefty fine. 
 Dealers were further directed to sell aerial display fireworks, including shells, rockets, Roman candles and cakes, only to people holding valid permits signed by an Inspector of Explosives. 
 Diwali, popularly known as the Festival of Lights, is one of the most important celebrations in the Hindu religion as it symbolises the triumph of light over darkness and good over evil. 
 The festival is traditionally marked by lighting oil lamps known as diyas, decorating homes, exchanging gifts, prayers, family gatherings, and fireworks displays. 
 The celebrations also coincide with the Hindu New Year in some Hindu traditions, marking the beginning of a new calendar year and a period of spiritual renewal. 
 In Kenya, Diwali is recognised under the Public Holidays Act as a public holiday for members of the Hindu faith, rather than a nationwide holiday observed by all Kenyans. 
 In 2024, President William Ruto pledged to formally make Diwali celebrations a national holiday that would be celebrated on November 1 of every year.
 However, the proposal has since remained unimplemented, with Diwali yet to be formally designated a nationwide public holiday and, as of November 2026, the celebrations remain a public holiday only for the Hindu faith.
